Messages.Author: Jasper Phillips
Messages.Body:
Ok, here's my second attempt at a voting deck. I decided to forego all
defense, and stick with only presence. People don't (yet!) play many
cards to hose majesty here, so it should survive combat.

The main idea is to call votes or bleed with PRE vamps, get blocked
and majesty to untap, then do the other option. Once I've gone through
twice with all of my larger vamps, I can run back through with the pre
ones. The Misdirection could also be key if you think your prey has
no untap.

Anyway, I'm not really sure how this will fare, and am looking for
advice.

-Jasper

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
Jasper Phillips (phil...@nd.ENGR.ORST.EDU) wrote:

[re: weenie presence vote deck]

: Perhaps you're right. I've kind of leaned that was as it is, but figured

: I'd run out of really small vamps with PRE, and that the titled ones were
: were worth it, since they were only a bit bigger, and had votes.

Well, the titled ones aren't so bad in some cases, but you gain a whole
lot in speed by using only the little guys. If I were going to play a
deck along these lines, I'd use a fair number of Presence master skill
cards; maybe 5-7 in a 90 card deck. There are at least two 1-cap
vamps with inferior presence (Igo, Antoinette Duchamp), a bunch of 2-caps,
and probably even more 3-caps, although you might want to just use the
1s, 2s, and Gideon Fontaine (PRE at 3). Steve "I bled someone for
14 pool in one turn because of a Misdirection" Wampler won Praxis: Ithaca
with a deck that was somewhat along these lines except that his was
weenie presence bleed instead of weenie presence vote.

This deck also makes very effective use of Info Highway. ;-)

: >besides, twenty majesty's gotta be overkill in just about anything that's
: >not a weenie deck...

: Really? I was planning on using 4-5 a turn... I figure it's hard to
: add too much if people don't play Immortal Grapple (I'm the only
: one that does here), since they're damn easy to get rid of. I figure
: even a deck without all weenies could use lots, since the bigger vampires
: will quite probably end up using 2 a turn.

Well, it could happen I guess. I think we're thinking of very different
situations here. In my playgroup, no one will be blocking much of
anything unless they're an intercept deck or something. And if they're
not an intercept deck but happen to have some vamps up who could block,
they're certainly not going to be intercepting votes at +1 stealth. So
when I play a vote deck, I only rarely use even 1 majesty a turn just
by doing actions; I use them when the omnipresent combat decks Bum Rush
me on my way to the forum. (And the Skins of Steel. Damn Immortal
Grapples.)

But anyway, it sounds like what you're envisioning is a situation where
your prey is a fairly heavy-blocking deck. In which case you could
indeed go through the Majesties pretty well. But around here twenty
would be an awful lot, because half the time you couldn't even play
them due to Immortal Grapple, and the rest of the time people wouldn't
be all that likely to be blocking you.

Josh

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Scott Halverson wrote:
"How many people in Jyhad-land play with the 4 card limit rule? My gaming
group swears by it in every deck we build. Decks with this many Majesties and
KRC's will wipe the table clean, so we have always played with the card limit.
Are there any other players who feel the same way, or are me and my gaming
group just out in left field?"

As you seem to be fairly new to this group, you would have no way to know that
the No Limit/Card Limit thread is one of the most common threads that comes up
around here (although there hasn't been one for a while). Yes, some people
play with Card Limits (CL, ususaly 4CL), but the game was designed to have no
limits on any cards in the deck, and card limits certainly do not fix the game
in any way. Don't get me wrong--if you like using card limits, go to town and
have a fine time, but the game was designed specifically to _not_ have card
limits, and with them it is a really different game than was intended.

Yes, card limits of some sort prevent people from using multiples of the more
severe cards in the set (like KRC and Majesty, for instance), but it also
prevents them from using multiples of the basic building blocks of the game,
like Bum's Rush, Bewitching Oration, and Cats Guidance, and without unlimited
access to cards like these, many, many decks simply cannot compete against
decks like Malkavian Stealth and Bleed (which is ususally the main reason that
people decide that 4CL is needed in the first place...). Under 4CL, you can't
build a reliable Bum's Rush combat deck, but a Malkavian Stealth and Bleed deck
is completely unhindered, so it will dominate play.

With the advent of Sabbat, and the "pretty much the same but slightly
different" cards in the set, 4CL is pretty much a non issue, as you can
effectively have 8 of any card you want (like 4 Bum's Rush and 4 Ambush; 4
Deflection and 4 Redirection; ect), but by sticking to the 4CL, you manage to
miss out on the subtle yet important differences between, say, Skin of Steel
and Superior Mettle. Under 4CL, you just use 4 of each. Under NL, you might
use 8 of one and none of the other, or 6 and 2. The possibilites are endless.

There are _many_ well written articles about why 4CL is a bad idea archived on
Mark and Judith's excellent Jyhad Page (and far fewer about why 4Cl is a good
idea...), so rather than going on here, I encourage you to check them out.

Peter D Bakija

Messages.Author: Jasper Phillips
Messages.Body:
In article <353400...@cptc.wisc.edu>,

Scott Halvorson <halv...@cptc.wisc.edu> wrote:
>
>How many people in Jyhad-land play with the 4 card limit rule? My
>gaming group swears by it in every deck we build. Decks with this many
>Majesties and KRC's will wipe the table clean, so we have always played
>with the card limit. Are there any other players who feel the same way,
>or are me and my gaming group just out in left field?

Mostly out in left field I think. I find that the game is actually more
balanced, and you see more variety in decks, without a card limit
(the game wasn't broken like it's predecesor).

For example, this deck doesn't sweep the table clean at all.
I built it, tried it, and got my ass whupped. Badly. I managed to
weaken my prey so that he was easier for my predator after I was ousted,
but that was about it.

Plenty of good articles in the past from people who can say it
better than I if you look around a bit. If anything people seem
not for play balance (as you suggest), but for variety. IMHO you
actually get less variety, since having many of a given card isn't
neccesarily better (the right mix is the key), and some decks
just aren't possible with 4CL (e.g. a grave robbing deck).

Anyway, I'm guessing (I could easily be wrong, but this seems to
be a trend among people I've met) that you haven't actually tried
NCL (no card limit), and simply carried the 4CL over from magic
(an entirely different game, which badly needed it when the rule
was made). Give NCL a shot, it really is better.

: telepathic misdirection back in. How much majesty do you suggest,
: and what should I put in instead? I'm really curious, because no
: one plays an effective vote deck locally.

In our local fairly combat-heavy environment, I often play something
like 8 majesty/12 Skin of Steel in an 80-card pre/for vote deck. 20
anti-combat cards may not be that excessive; it's just that having them
all be Majesties may get you in trouble. (It would around here. ;-)
And by its nature, Majesty is only needed once per fight, and at
superior tends to be less necessary later in the turn (because your
opponents are tapped and you're not). So it's a very card-efficient
anti-combat card. Which is why it's so popular, of course. (Lately
Earth Meld has been making a local comeback as the even more efficient
cousin, annoying people left and right in Peter's all-Protean deck...)

I might play say 16 Majesty and put in 4 telepathic misdirection; I
don't recall exactly how many cards are in your deck, but if it's 80
I think that might be about right.

You might want to try playing some Mind Numbs if you have them; one
person played a tap and bleed presence deck here a while back, and it
worked fairly well. Should fit into a vote/bleed strategy decently
at least.

But if you can, I still think you should make the weenie-presence-vote
deck. ;-)

Josh

Messages.Author: badger
Messages.Body:
I find the people who cry the loudest for card limits in Jyhad are just
the worst players (no offense). As with most things in life, if you
have too much of a good thing, it can kill you. When a player has
muliples of a single card it simply means he has less of something
else. Find out what that something is and figure out a way to exploit
it. Or talk to you fellow disgruntled Methuselahs and team up on the
bastard. That should teach him a lesson.

If someone is pure stealth/bleed, they don't have intercept or politics.
If someone is all combat, they don't have bleed or politics.
If someone is all politics, they can't fight or block.

In short, stop shedding tears and start fighting back!

Badger

>It's not that we are actually all that bad either. I've been playing Jyhad

>going to lose. Sure I can try and put minion attack cards, i.e. B.Rush, but
>that only go's so far. It also makes for a much more enjoyable game.

I'm slightly confused. Where's the cheese in no-limits play? If someone's
packing heavy Strike: Combat Ends, you can (a) Immortal Grapple [the
preferred hoser], (b) Psyche!/Hidden Lurker/Fast Reaction, or (c) avoid
getting into combat.

The key to no-limits play is to strike at the weak points. There are always
weak points in a no-limits deck. Either you pack lots of what you need,
in which case you're vulnerable to what you left out, or you've packed a
little of everything, in which case what you need isn't reliably available.

> With 5 players (our usual group.) that's a max deck of 90 cards. Sure you
>could put in 10 copies of 9 cards and make sure you get what you want, and
>more than likely win. But with a deck with 2 of one card, 3 of another, and 4
>of another one, and so on then the deck is much more veried. God forbide that
>you actually have to take some time and think about what will go in to fill
>the other spaces, but it does happen.

The most effective decks have the smallest amount of discrete card types in
them, and maximize the amount of copies of these. An archetypal Brujah
deck, for example, features:

15xBum's Rush
15xTorn Signpost
15xFlash
15xImmortal Grapple
15xBlur
15xMasters 3x(Potence, Celerity, Hunting Ground, Blood Doll, Info H'way)

This is nice and reliable. It's also strongly vulnerable to vote and
stealth bleed, especially weenie variants thereon. That's 5 distinct card
types (not counting masters).

>If I wanted to continue to play a game with a small deck size and and lots'o
>cheese I would play Rage.

Well, other folx have pointed out that Sabbat brings no-limit V:tES and
card-limit V:tES quite a bit closer, except that decisions that are
strategic/tactically based in no-limit (8 Skin of Steel? 6 SoS and 2
Superior Mettle?) become automatic in limit (4 of each). The effect
of this is to quash the subtle difference between similar cards, and that
robs the game of much of its flavor.

I'm not going to explore the limit v. no-limit debate in greater depth
than this -- it's been hashed out thoroughly in the past, and arguments
on both sides have been archived on the web.

gomi

The point is, though, a deck with 10 copies of 9 cards each is going to lose
pretty often. There are just so many situations in Jyhad that you have to
deal with: bad crypt draw, rush defense, vote defense, bleed defense,
Corruption, minion degradation (as seen in Vicissitude and, to a lesser
degree, Dementation and Quietus), nasty locations, contestation... The list
goes on and on. The best decks have a little of defense for almost anything.
You know... maybe you add a Recruitment in case a situation comes up where
you desperately need Muaziz, or you add 2 Arsons to take out an Elysium if
necessary, an SR to kill a crucial Giant's Blood or Vulnerability, a couple of
Wakes to stop unstealthed bleeds. The list goes on and on here as well.

And so, it's good to be diverse. At the same time, it's obvious that many
strategies are hosed by a 4 CL or even a 6 CL. Corruption can't work. With
4CL, you'll maybe get a small vampire if you draw them all at the beginning.
Potence combat, in general, only survives because of Immortal Grapple, because
it uses too many cards per strike to deal with S:CE any other way. On the
other hand, a good Gangrel deck should be able to laugh at the average Majesty
deck. You *will* run out of Majesties, and Haven Uncovereds, even if burned
as soon as possible, can get you a good 3 attacks per turn.

If you're going to play 4 CL, you might as well just check everyone's deck for
S&B and give all victory points to the person who uses the most variations of
Kine Dominance, GtU, Scouting Mission, Bonding, Threats, Foreshadowing
Destruction, Conditioning, and Command of the Beast. Maybe give special
allowance for the Malkavian who realizes that Pulse of the Canaille is also
available via in-clan discipline.

NCL gives the possibility of a combat deck, which needs many multiples of
Bum's Rush and Ambush, to do well in a game. In fact, when you really look at
it, the deck which is hurt most by 4 CL (besides Corruption which is not
viable at all) is the combat deck. Sure, the voting decks use Majesty, but
there's still Staredown and Catatonic Fear, not to mention disciplineless
dodges and then for the Ventrue, plenty of instances of damage prevention.
The combat deck still must rely on Bum's Rush, Ambush, and Haven Uncovered
(it's generally counter-productive to put more than 5 Havens in a deck, which
is why I don't mention them as being necessary in excess of card limit).
Combat decks, however, are by far not the most powerful decks at tournaments.
The usual winners are stealth bleed (which is amazingly easy to do under 4
CL), and occasionally big vamp vote/bleed. The big vamp decks may use 10
Majesties, but they could do almost just as well with 4 Majesty, 4 Catatonic
Fear, and 2 Staredown.

The only thing it would do to require the above (4 of each useful card,
instead of 8 of one card and 2 of another, or whatever), would be to reduce
creativity. No longer do you have the Gangrel wondering "Do I need the
maneuver from Claws of the Dead, or the press from Wolf Claws? Or should I
plan on damage prevention and use Bone Spur?" Instead, the Gangrel says, "All
right! Sabbat came out, so now I can use 12 Claws instead of 8. 4 of each."

-Chris

I agree, Jyhad is balanced enough that if you load a deck to heavily one way it
weakens that deck in antoher area. If you make huge decks them you statistically
reduce the chance of getting the cards you want.The entire objective here is
strategy, in both the building of a deck and the useage of such. Not only does the
inherent limitations of a one sided deck become apparent in a game when all you do
is one action (bleed for instance) but the other players that might be your victims
in a few minutes dont appreciate the fact that you have just killed you 3rd prey by
bleeding them for 11 and hey "I'm gonna be his prey in a second". I personally
attempt to quell the largest threat at the table (short term) and screw my prey in
the process (long term). Our group uses no limits (cards or total decks size). Do
what you want, its always a trade-off.

Messages.Author: Jeffrey Thompson
Messages.Body:
How do you keep new players?

Any player that is relatively new to the game is simply going to be
intimidated
if you pull out a deck with 8 IG or whatever rare is your card of choice.

Most of the groups that I have played with that used card limits used them
to encourage the players with 20 of every card to play decks that would be
competitive with the decks of players who only had access to 3 or 4 of any
particular card.

Another reason many people play with card limits is that they don't know
about NRA. Without the No Repeat Actions tournament rule, certain deck
types will always dominate. Any PRO/dom deck or PRE deck that can take
unlimited actions until they succeed will be more effective than a deck that
cannot afford to tap out every turn.

Anyway, how do you keep new players?????

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Jeffery Thompson wrote:
"Any player that is relatively new to the game is simply going to be
intimidated
if you pull out a deck with 8 IG or whatever rare is your card of choice."

But they are going to be just as intimidated by a CL based Malkavian S+B deck.
The card limits don't keep new players from being intimidated by seasoned
players with a million cards. If you don't want to intimidate new players,
either let them learn how to play with decks you have built, or handycap
yourself with a goofy deck design. Once they consistently kill your goofy
deck, start using a better one.

Teaching people to play with card limits for the purposes of making the game
nicer will accomplish little more than encourage them to all figure out how to
play S+B decks, which is fine, but there are countless other deck strategies
that are effective with no card limits that are completely hamstrung by card
limits.

"Most of the groups that I have played with that used card limits used them to
encourage the players with 20 of every card to play decks that would be
competitive with the decks of players who only had access to 3 or 4 of any
particular card."

At this point in time, there is really no reason for people to not have access
to close to an infinte number of Jyhad cards. Our group just purchased 13
boxes of boosters from the Edge Man in CA for less than 5 bucks a box. Heck, I
bought a $5.00 box of boosters just to pull out 36 rares and give away the
commons (you generally need multiples of commons, not rares) to the new folks.

Messages.Author: Lambach
Messages.Body:
> Ok, perhaps "worst" isn't the word I was looking for, but I think your
> and my points are on the same target. What I meant is don't focus on
> the fact your enemy has 20 Wakes or 20 Majesties. Think instead that
> said person has no stealth or no politics. Whatever the case may be,
> Jyhad is balanced enough that one deck type cannot dominate for long.
>

> Badger

It seems to me that we are concerned by entirely different matters.
When you write "Jyhad is balanced enough that one deck type cannot
dominate for long.", you assume that we card-limit babies are worried
about losing to stronger decks. It is not necessarily so. If my prey or
predator has 20 Wakes or 20 Majesties, and I decide to beat him with
stealth or politics, I'm in for a dull & extremely boring evening
(IMHO). So your suggestion doesn't solve my problem at all.
Now why play under 4-card limits? It is a rather easy way to limit some
"automatic" combinations (Thoughts Betrayed + Torn Signpost + Pulled
Fangs, for instance, gets pretty tiring after a while). Does it limit
the decks we play? Of course it does. Is this a bad thing? It depends.
Sometimes, yes (Temptation decks can be difficult to build if you only
had 1 box of AH, for instance). Sometimes, no. I believe that it is very
profitable and interesting to build decks under such a constraint. And
you don't get stuck when you get a prey or predator who happens to have
exactly the deck he needs against you (as in your example, Badger). Oh
yes, I forgot: we have a hell of a good time playing with these
baby-decks. I guess that makes it worth it?

L-R

PS: I'd like to add we do not consider ourselves to be "unexperienced"
players. Our first game of Jyhad occured 72 hours after the French
release of the original set. (ever played a sealed-deck tournament with
one starter and three boosters? It was just great.)
